# The CL2 covariance {#sec-app-cl2}

Notation follows the main text: $\mathbf W$ holds the working weights
$w_{ij} = (d\mu/d\eta)^2_{ij}/\{\phi V(\mu_{ij})\}$, $\mathbf S = \sum_r (\lambda_r/\phi)\mathbf S_r$,
$\mathbf V_p = (\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X + \mathbf S)^{-1}$,
$\mathbf V_e = \mathbf V_p\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X\mathbf V_p$, and for curve $i$
$\tilde{\mathbf X}_i = \mathbf W_i^{1/2}\mathbf X_i$ and
$z_{ij} = (y_{ij} - \hat\mu_{ij})/\{\phi V(\hat\mu_{ij})\}^{1/2}$.
The stacked whitened design is $\tilde{\mathbf X}$, and
$\tilde{\mathbf H} = \tilde{\mathbf X}\mathbf V_p\tilde{\mathbf X}^\top$ has blocks
$\tilde{\mathbf H}_{ih}$.

## Scores and the penalized bread

For an exponential-family response the score of the log-likelihood contribution of $y_{ij}$ is
$$
\mathbf s_{ij}(\boldsymbol\theta)
= \frac{(y_{ij} - \mu_{ij})\,(d\mu/d\eta)_{ij}}{\phi V(\mu_{ij})}\,\mathbf x_{ij}
= z_{ij}\,\tilde{\mathbf x}_{ij},
\qquad \tilde{\mathbf x}_{ij} = w_{ij}^{1/2}\mathbf x_{ij},
$$ {#eq-s1-score}
so the score of curve $i$ is $\mathbf u_i = \sum_j \mathbf s_{ij} = \tilde{\mathbf X}_i^\top\mathbf z_i$.
The fit maximizes $\sum_{i,j}\ell_{ij}(\boldsymbol\theta) - \tfrac12\boldsymbol\theta^\top\mathbf S\boldsymbol\theta$,
whose estimating equation is
$$
\sum_{i=1}^G \mathbf u_i(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}) = \mathbf S\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}.
$$ {#eq-s1-ee}
The negative Hessian of the penalized log-likelihood is $\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X + \mathbf S = \mathbf V_p^{-1}$ (exactly for canonical links, in expectation otherwise). Linearizing @eq-s1-ee around the target $\boldsymbol\theta^*$ at which its expectation vanishes gives
$$
\hat{\boldsymbol\theta} - \boldsymbol\theta^* \approx \mathbf V_p \sum_{i=1}^G \{\mathbf u_i(\boldsymbol\theta^*) - \mathrm E\,\mathbf u_i(\boldsymbol\theta^*)\},
\qquad
\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}) \approx \mathbf V_p \Bigl\{\sum_{i=1}^G \mathrm{Var}\,\mathbf u_i(\boldsymbol\theta^*)\Bigr\}\mathbf V_p ,
$$ {#eq-s1-lin}
so $\mathbf V_p$ is the bread and only the meat $\sum_i\mathrm{Var}\,\mathbf u_i$ depends on the
within-curve dependence. Under the working model, $\mathrm{Var}(\mathbf z_i) = \mathbf I$ and the
meat is $\tilde{\mathbf X}^\top\tilde{\mathbf X}$, which returns $\mathbf V_e$. The unpenalized bread
$(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X)^{-1}$ linearizes a different estimator. Scores and penalty are
both on the scale of the summed log-likelihood; a construction that averages the scores over the
$N$ observations must use the penalty $\sum_r\lambda_r\mathbf S_r/(N\phi)$, or the bread and the
shrinkage are mis-scaled by the factor $N$ (and by $\phi$ if it is dropped).

By @eq-s1-ee the curve scores at the estimate do not sum to zero: $\sum_i \tilde{\mathbf X}_i^\top\mathbf z_i = \mathbf S\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$.
Unlike the unpenalized cluster sandwich [@LiangZeger1986], whose curve scores at the estimate sum
to zero, the meat $\sum_i\mathbf U_i\mathbf U_i^\top$ below is not centered; Proposition A.1(b)
gives the consequence.

## The leverage adjustment

The CL2 covariance of the main text is
$$
\hat{\mathbf V}_{\mathrm{CL2}} = \frac{G}{G-1}\,\mathbf V_p\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^G\mathbf U_i\mathbf U_i^\top\Bigr)\mathbf V_p + (\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_e),
\qquad
\mathbf U_i = \tilde{\mathbf X}_i^\top\mathbf R_i^{-1/2}\mathbf z_i ,
$$ {#eq-s1-cl2}
with $\mathbf R_i = [(\mathbf I - \tilde{\mathbf H})(\mathbf I - \tilde{\mathbf H})^\top]_{ii}$.
Since $\tilde{\mathbf X}^\top\tilde{\mathbf X} = \mathbf V_p^{-1} - \mathbf S$,
$(\mathbf I - \tilde{\mathbf H})^2 = \mathbf I - \tilde{\mathbf X}(2\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_p\tilde{\mathbf X}^\top\tilde{\mathbf X}\mathbf V_p)\tilde{\mathbf X}^\top$ and
$$
\mathbf R_i
= \mathbf I - \tilde{\mathbf X}_i\bigl(2\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_p\tilde{\mathbf X}^\top\tilde{\mathbf X}\mathbf V_p\bigr)\tilde{\mathbf X}_i^\top
= \mathbf I - \tilde{\mathbf H}_{ii} - \tilde{\mathbf X}_i\mathbf V_p\mathbf S\mathbf V_p\tilde{\mathbf X}_i^\top .
$$ {#eq-s1-Rg}
$\mathbf R_i$ needs only $\tilde{\mathbf X}_i$ and one $p\times p$ matrix. It is computed in the
column space of $\tilde{\mathbf X}_i$ in $\mathbb R^{D_i}$ (dimension at most $\min(D_i, p)$), because
$\mathbf R_i$ equals $\mathbf I$ on its orthogonal complement and $\tilde{\mathbf X}_i^\top$ annihilates
that complement.

*Relation to CR2.* The bias-reduced linearization of @BellMcCaffrey2002 chooses $\mathbf A_i$ with
$\mathbf A_i[(\mathbf I - \mathbf H)\boldsymbol\Phi(\mathbf I - \mathbf H)^\top]_{ii}\mathbf A_i = \boldsymbol\Phi_i$
for a working covariance $\boldsymbol\Phi$ [@McCaffreyBell2006; @PustejovskyTipton2018]. With
$\boldsymbol\Phi = \mathbf I$ this is $\mathbf A_i = \mathbf R_i^{-1/2}$. For a projection,
$\mathbf R_i = \mathbf I - \mathbf H_{ii}$ and the usual CR2 results. The penalized hat is not
idempotent: the last term of @eq-s1-Rg is positive semidefinite, so
$\mathbf R_i \preceq \mathbf I - \tilde{\mathbf H}_{ii}$, and the approximation
$\mathbf A^{\mathrm s}_i = (\mathbf I - \tilde{\mathbf H}_{ii})^{-1/2}$, which keeps the full block
$\tilde{\mathbf H}_{ii}$ but drops the last term of @eq-s1-Rg (the *shortcut*),
under-corrects: $\mathbf A^{\mathrm s}_i\mathbf R_i\mathbf A^{\mathrm s}_i \preceq \mathbf I$. The
dropped term is small when the per-curve leverage is small.

*Expectation of the meat.* Take the Gaussian working model with fixed $\boldsymbol\lambda$ and fixed design:
$\mathbf W^{1/2}\mathbf y = \tilde{\mathbf X}\boldsymbol\theta + \boldsymbol\varepsilon$ with
$\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon) = \mathbf I$. Then
$\mathbf z = (\mathbf I - \tilde{\mathbf H})(\tilde{\mathbf X}\boldsymbol\theta + \boldsymbol\varepsilon)$,
and $(\mathbf I - \tilde{\mathbf H})\tilde{\mathbf X} = \tilde{\mathbf X}\mathbf V_p\mathbf S$ gives
$$
\mathrm E(\mathbf z_i) = \mathbf m_i = \tilde{\mathbf X}_i\mathbf V_p\mathbf S\boldsymbol\theta,
\qquad
\mathrm E(\mathbf z_i\mathbf z_i^\top) = \mathbf R_i + \mathbf m_i\mathbf m_i^\top .
$$ {#eq-s1-mean}
The penalized residuals have nonzero mean unless $\mathbf S\boldsymbol\theta = \mathbf 0$. With
$\mathbf R_i$ invertible and the floor inactive,
$$
\mathrm E\Bigl(\sum_i\mathbf U_i\mathbf U_i^\top\Bigr)
= \sum_i \tilde{\mathbf X}_i^\top\tilde{\mathbf X}_i
+ \sum_i \tilde{\mathbf X}_i^\top\mathbf R_i^{-1/2}\mathbf m_i\mathbf m_i^\top\mathbf R_i^{-1/2}\tilde{\mathbf X}_i .
$$ {#eq-s1-unbiased}
The first term is the working-model sampling meat, $\mathrm{Var}(\tilde{\mathbf X}^\top\boldsymbol\varepsilon)$,
so $\mathbf V_p(\sum_i\mathbf U_i\mathbf U_i^\top)\mathbf V_p$ is unbiased for $\mathbf V_e$ when the
truth lies in the null space of the penalty and biased upwards by a positive semidefinite term
otherwise. The factor $G/(G-1)$ adds a further upward bias. Under within-curve dependence,
$\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon_i) = \boldsymbol\Sigma_i \neq \mathbf I$, and the adjustment
removes the residual shrinkage only approximately; it does not whiten correlated residuals.

*Floor and factor.* The eigenvalues of $\mathbf R_i$ are floored at $10^{-6}$ before the inverse
square root, which caps the inflation of any residual direction at a factor $10^3$. The floor binds
only for curves whose data nearly determine a coefficient direction on their own; how often it
bound in the studies was not recorded. CR2 carries no
factor $G/(G-1)$; we keep it. The factor inflates frequentist CL2 standard errors by
`r f(100 * (sqrt(40 / 39) - 1), 1)`% at $G = 40$ and `r f(100 * (sqrt(100 / 99) - 1), 1)`% at
$G = 100$; in the Bayesian form it multiplies only the sandwich part, so these are upper bounds.

CR1 is @eq-s1-cl2 with $\mathbf R_i = \mathbf I$ and no further degrees-of-freedom
factor.

## Bayesian and frequentist forms

The frequentist form omits $\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_e = \mathbf V_p\mathbf S\mathbf V_p$. For
Gaussian responses with identity link and fixed $\boldsymbol\lambda$, the bias of
$\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$ is $-\mathbf V_p\mathbf S\boldsymbol\theta$. Under the smoothing prior
$\boldsymbol\theta \sim N(\mathbf 0, \mathbf S^-)$,
$\mathrm E(\mathbf V_p\mathbf S\boldsymbol\theta\boldsymbol\theta^\top\mathbf S\mathbf V_p) = \mathbf V_p\mathbf S\mathbf V_p$:
the allowance is the prior-averaged squared bias, and $\mathbf V_p$ the prior-averaged mean squared
error matrix [@Wahba1983; @Nychka1988; @MarraWood2012]. For a fixed truth and any contrast
$\mathbf a$, by the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality,
$$
(\mathbf a^\top\mathbf V_p\mathbf S\boldsymbol\theta)^2 \le (\mathbf a^\top\mathbf V_p\mathbf S\mathbf V_p\mathbf a)\,(\boldsymbol\theta^\top\mathbf S\boldsymbol\theta),
\qquad \boldsymbol\theta^\top\mathbf S\boldsymbol\theta = \sum_r (\lambda_r/\phi)\,\boldsymbol\theta^\top\mathbf S_r\boldsymbol\theta .
$$ {#eq-s1-cs}
The allowance bounds the squared bias of every contrast if
$\boldsymbol\theta^\top\mathbf S\boldsymbol\theta \le 1$; for larger values the bound permits,
but does not imply, a bias above the allowance.

Where the data identify $\boldsymbol\theta$
($\tilde{\mathbf X}^\top\tilde{\mathbf X}$ positive definite), the squared bias scales as
$\lambda^2$ and the allowance as $\lambda$ for small $\boldsymbol\lambda$. Undersmoothing, as REML
produces under within-curve dependence, therefore makes the allowance large relative to the bias but
small relative to the dependence-inflated variance, and the two forms nearly coincide. For a truth
that is rough at the selected $\boldsymbol\lambda$ ($\boldsymbol\theta^\top\mathbf S\boldsymbol\theta$
large), or after oversmoothing, the bias can exceed the allowance, most likely where the truth is most
curved. Under independent errors with a smooth
truth the allowance exceeds the bias and the Bayesian form overcovers.

## Extended families

The CL2 construction needs a factorization $\mathbf s_{ij} = z_{ij}\tilde{\mathbf x}_{ij}$ in which
$\tilde{\mathbf x}_{ij}$ carries the Fisher weight of the fit, so that
$\operatorname{tr}\tilde{\mathbf H}$ equals the effective degrees of freedom.

*Gaussian location--scale* (mgcv's gaulss). The two linear predictors $\eta_1$ (mean) and
$\eta_2$ (inverse standard deviation $\tau$) have block-diagonal Fisher information with weights
$W_1 = \tau^2(d\mu/d\eta_1)^2$ and $W_2 = 2(d\tau/d\eta_2)^2/\tau^2$. Each observation contributes
two pseudo-rows, both assigned to its curve,
$$
\tilde{\mathbf x}_{k} = W_k^{1/2}\mathbf x_{k}, \qquad z_k = \frac{\partial\ell/\partial\eta_k}{W_k^{1/2}}, \qquad k = 1, 2,
$$ {#eq-s1-gaulss}
with $\partial\ell/\partial\eta_1 = \tau^2(y - \mu)\,d\mu/d\eta_1$ and
$\partial\ell/\partial\eta_2 = (1/\tau - \tau(y-\mu)^2)\,d\tau/d\eta_2$; $\mathbf x_k$ is the
design row of predictor $k$, zero in the other block.

*Scaled t* (scat). With degrees of freedom $\nu$ and scale $\sigma$ at their estimates, the exact
location score and Fisher weight are
$$
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\mu} = \frac{(\nu + 1)(y - \mu)}{\nu\sigma^2 + (y - \mu)^2},
\qquad
W = \Bigl(\frac{d\mu}{d\eta}\Bigr)^2\frac{\nu + 1}{(\nu + 3)\sigma^2},
$$ {#eq-s1-scat}
and $z = (\partial\ell/\partial\mu)(d\mu/d\eta)/W^{1/2}$. The working-residual score
@eq-s1-score would treat the $t$ response as Gaussian and give no downweighting of outliers.

All other extended families of mgcv (negative binomial, Tweedie, beta, ordered categorical) use the
working-residual score @eq-s1-score with the fitted variance function. For the negative binomial,
with its shape parameter at the estimate, this is the exact score for the mean; for the beta family
it is an approximation. The simulation uses CL2 for the beta and negative-binomial responses. Families that define their own sandwich
(multinomial) have no cluster-robust covariance.

## Asymptotic validity for fixed smoothing parameters

**Proposition A.1.** *Assume (i) the curves $(\mathbf y_i, \mathbf X_i)$, $i = 1,\dots,G$, are
independent and identically distributed with $D_i \le \bar D < \infty$, with arbitrary dependence
within a curve; (ii) the basis, hence $p$, is fixed and the link is canonical; (iii)
$\boldsymbol\lambda = \boldsymbol\lambda_G$ is non-random with $\mathbf S_G/G \to \mathbf S_\infty$;
(iv) the weighted design rows are uniformly bounded, the curve scores have bounded moments of
order $2 + \delta$ and dominated derivatives near the target, and $\mathbf J = \mathrm E(\tilde{\mathbf X}_1^\top\tilde{\mathbf X}_1) + \mathbf S_\infty$
is positive definite at $\boldsymbol\theta^*_\infty = \lim_G \boldsymbol\theta^*_G$, where
$\boldsymbol\theta^*_G$ solves*
$$
\mathrm E\,\mathbf u_1(\boldsymbol\theta) = (\mathbf S_G/G)\,\boldsymbol\theta .
$$ {#eq-s1-target}
*Then (a) $\sqrt G(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta} - \boldsymbol\theta^*_G) \to N(\mathbf 0, \mathbf J^{-1}\mathbf M\mathbf J^{-1})$
with $\mathbf M = \mathrm{Var}\,\mathbf u_1(\boldsymbol\theta^*_\infty)$. (b) With
$\boldsymbol\mu = \mathrm E\,\mathbf u_1(\boldsymbol\theta^*_\infty) = \mathbf S_\infty\boldsymbol\theta^*_\infty$,
the variance part of @eq-s1-cl2 (and of CR1) satisfies*
$$
G\,\frac{G}{G-1}\,\mathbf V_p\Bigl(\sum_i\mathbf U_i\mathbf U_i^\top\Bigr)\mathbf V_p \;\to_p\; \mathbf J^{-1}(\mathbf M + \boldsymbol\mu\boldsymbol\mu^\top)\mathbf J^{-1},
\qquad
G(\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_e) \to \mathbf J^{-1}\mathbf S_\infty\mathbf J^{-1},
$$ {#eq-s1-cov}
*so the variance part is consistent for the covariance in (a) if $\mathbf S_\infty\boldsymbol\theta^*_\infty = \mathbf 0$
and conservative otherwise; the Bayesian form adds $\mathbf J^{-1}\mathbf S_\infty\mathbf J^{-1}$.
(c) If the mean model is correct and
$\sqrt G(\boldsymbol\theta^*_G - \boldsymbol\theta) \to \mathbf 0$ (which forces
$\mathbf S_\infty\boldsymbol\theta = \mathbf 0$ even if $\mathbf S_\infty \neq \mathbf 0$), the frequentist CL2 interval for
any fixed contrast is asymptotically valid for the true $\boldsymbol\theta$, and the Bayesian one is
valid and conservative, asymptotically exact if $\mathbf S_\infty = \mathbf 0$.*

For Gaussian responses with identity link, the finite-sample target given the design is
$\mathrm E(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}) = (\mathbf I - \mathbf V_p\mathbf S)\boldsymbol\theta$, of which
@eq-s1-target is the population version; for GLMs the target solves the expected penalized score
equation.

*Proof.* $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$ solves an M-estimating equation with independent curve
contributions and a deterministic penalty offset whose expectation vanishes at
$\boldsymbol\theta^*_G$; (a) follows from the standard argument for such equations
[@LiangZeger1986; @HansenLee2019]. For (b), bounded curve sizes and fixed $p$ make the leverages
$O_p(G^{-1})$, so CL2 and CR1 meats agree to first order, and the meat converges to the second moment
of a score with mean $\boldsymbol\mu$. For (c), a correct mean model gives curve scores with mean
zero whatever the dependence within the curve. $\square$

The proposition does not cover smoothing parameters selected from the data, nor a number of
coefficients comparable to or larger than $G$; both hold in our applications and simulations.

## Covariance components

```{r s1-ablation-data}
s1_cells <- readr::read_csv("ablation/summaries/ablation-cells.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
s1_contr <- readr::read_csv("ablation/summaries/ablation-contrasts.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
s1_err <- c(iid = "independent", ou = "rough stationary", fpc = "smooth")
s1_design <- DESIGN |> filter(cell %in% unique(s1_cells$cell))
s1_arms <- tibble::tribble(
  ~arm, ~crit, ~label,
  "model", "z", "model",
  "cr1_b", "z", "CR1",
  "cl2s_b", "z", "CL2 $I - H$",
  "cl2e_b", "z", "CL2",
  "cl2e_f", "z", "CL2 freq.",
  "cl2e_b", "t", "CL2 $t_{G-1}$",
  "fix_cl2e_b", "z", "CL2 fixed $\\lambda$"
)
s1_cov_tab <- \(e) {
  s1_cells |>
    filter(estimand == e) |>
    inner_join(s1_arms, by = c("arm", "crit")) |>
    mutate(label = factor(label, s1_arms$label), family = label_family(family), error = s1_err[error]) |>
    select(family, error, G, label, coverage) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = label, values_from = coverage, names_sort = TRUE) |>
    arrange(family, factor(error, s1_err), G) |>
    mutate(family = as.character(family), error = as.character(error))
}
s1_kable <- \(d) {
  dup_err <- duplicated(paste(d$family, d$error))
  d$family[duplicated(d$family)] <- ""
  d$error[dup_err] <- ""
  knitr::kable(d, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, digits = 3, escape = FALSE, linesep = "")
}
s1_ct <- \(ct, dep, g, e = c("mean", "beta")) {
  d <- s1_contr |> filter(contrast == ct, estimand %in% e, (error != "iid") == dep, G == g)
  c(diff = mean(d$diff), se_lo = min(d$diff_se), se_hi = max(d$diff_se))
}
s1_cta <- \(a, dep, g, e = "beta", crit = "z") {
  mean(s1_cells$coverage[s1_cells$arm == a & s1_cells$crit == crit & s1_cells$estimand %in% e & (s1_cells$error != "iid") == dep & s1_cells$G %in% g])
}
s1_cell <- \(e, a, fam, err, g) {
  s1_cells$coverage[s1_cells$estimand == e & s1_cells$arm == a & s1_cells$crit == "z" & s1_cells$family == fam & s1_cells$error == err & s1_cells$G == g]
}
s1_sesd <- \(a, dep, g, e = "beta") {
  mean(s1_cells$se_sd_ratio[s1_cells$arm == a & s1_cells$crit == "z" & s1_cells$estimand == e & (s1_cells$error != "iid") == dep & s1_cells$G == g])
}
```

The comparison uses the `r nrow(s1_design)` main factorial settings at the default signal level
($D =$ `r unique(s1_design$D)`, $G$ = `r paste(sort(unique(s1_design$G)), collapse = " or ")`,
`r unique(s1_cells$n_rep)` replicates per setting) with common random numbers. Except for the fixed-$\lambda$ interval, every covariance is computed for the
same REML fit of each replicate; these fits reproduce the stored fits of the main study to numerical
precision. The intervals are the model-based interval ($\mathbf V_c$); CR1, CL2 with the
$\mathbf I - \tilde{\mathbf H}_{ii}$ approximation, and CL2, all in the Bayesian form of @eq-s1-cl2; CL2 in the frequentist form; CL2 with the critical
value $t_{G-1,0.975}$ in place of $z_{0.975}$; and CL2 after a refit of the same data with the
smoothing parameters fixed, per penalty, at the geometric mean of the setting's REML estimates.
The fixed-$\lambda$ refit removes the replicate-to-replicate variability of the smoothing parameters
and also moves them to their typical level. @fig-s1-beta, @fig-s1-mean and @fig-s1-alpha-gamma show
the coverage, @fig-s1-contrasts the paired differences; Supplement S7 lists the values.

```{r}
#| label: fig-s1-beta
#| fig-cap: "Covariance components, $\\beta(s,t)$: grid-averaged coverage of nominal 95% pointwise intervals by family, error process and number of curves $G$, main factorial settings at the default signal level, 200 replicates. Model-based: $\\mathbf V_c$; CR1, CL2, shortcut (CL2 with the $\\mathbf I - \\tilde{\\mathbf H}_{ii}$ approximation) and CL2 in the Bayesian form; CL2, frequentist: frequentist form; CL2, t(G-1): CL2 with $t$ critical value; CL2, fixed $\\lambda$: CL2 after a refit with smoothing parameters fixed at the setting's geometric-mean REML values. Arrows at the left edge mark coverage below the axis range; the values are printed next to them. Dashed: 0.95."
#| fig-height: 4.6
fig_s1_cov(s1_long(s1_cells, s1_arms, "beta"), "error")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-s1-mean
#| fig-cap: "Covariance components, mean $\\mathrm E(Y \\mid X)$: grid-averaged coverage of nominal 95% pointwise intervals; intervals, settings and marks as in @fig-s1-beta."
#| fig-height: 4.6
fig_s1_cov(s1_long(s1_cells, s1_arms, "mean"), "error")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-s1-contrasts
#| fig-cap: "Covariance components: paired coverage differences in percentage points, averaged over families and over the mean and $\\beta(s,t)$, by error process and number of curves $G$. Each difference compares two intervals on the same replicates; unless stated, both are CL2 in the Bayesian form with the normal critical value. Shortcut: the $\\mathbf I - \\tilde{\\mathbf H}_{ii}$ approximation. The SE of the averages cannot be recovered from the retained per-setting summaries, because the settings share replicates; the range of the per-setting paired Monte Carlo SEs is in Supplement S7."
#| fig-height: 2.5
fig_s1_contrasts(s1_ct)
```

Under dependence the leverage adjustment adds
`r pp(s1_ct("CL2 - CR1", TRUE, 40)[["diff"]])` of coverage over CR1 at $G = 40$ and
`r pp(s1_ct("CL2 - CR1", TRUE, 100)[["diff"]])` at $G = 100$; the full block adds at most
`r pp(max(s1_contr$diff[s1_contr$contrast == "exact - shortcut" & s1_contr$estimand %in% c("mean", "beta")]))`
in any setting over the $\mathbf I - \tilde{\mathbf H}_{ii}$ approximation (under dependence
`r rng_pp(s1_contr$diff[s1_contr$contrast == "exact - shortcut" & s1_contr$estimand %in% c("mean", "beta") & s1_contr$error != "iid"])`),
in line with
$\mathbf A^{\mathrm s}_i\mathbf R_i\mathbf A^{\mathrm s}_i \preceq \mathbf I$. The allowance $\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_e$ matters
under independent errors (`r pp(s1_ct("Bayes - freq (CL2)", FALSE, 40)[["diff"]])` at $G = 40$),
much less under dependence (`r pp(s1_ct("Bayes - freq (CL2)", TRUE, 40)[["diff"]])`).

With reselected smoothing parameters, the grid average of CL2's root-mean-square
standard error divided by the empirical standard deviation of $\hat\beta$ under dependence is `r f(s1_sesd("cl2e_b", TRUE, 40), 2)` at $G = 40$ and
`r f(s1_sesd("cl2e_b", TRUE, 100), 2)` at $G = 100$; with fixed smoothing parameters it is
`r f(s1_sesd("fix_cl2e_b", TRUE, 40), 2)` and `r f(s1_sesd("fix_cl2e_b", TRUE, 100), 2)`, and CL2
coverage of $\beta$ rises from `r f(s1_cta("cl2e_b", TRUE, 40), 3)` to
`r f(s1_cta("fix_cl2e_b", TRUE, 40), 3)` at $G = 40$. Fixing the smoothing parameters, which @eq-s1-cl2 conditions on, at their typical level closes most
of the remaining shortfall at $G = 40$; the $t_{G-1}$ critical value recovers
`r pp(s1_ct("t - z (CL2)", TRUE, 40)[["diff"]])` of it.

Fixed smoothing parameters also raise CL2
coverage of $\alpha(t)$ and $\gamma(t)$ under dependence (@fig-s1-alpha-gamma): for binary responses with smooth errors at
$G = 40$, CL2 coverage of $\alpha(t)$ rises from `r f(s1_cell("alpha", "cl2e_b", "binomial", "fpc", 40), 3)`
to `r f(s1_cell("alpha", "fix_cl2e_b", "binomial", "fpc", 40), 3)` and that of $\gamma(t)$ from
`r f(s1_cell("gamma", "cl2e_b", "binomial", "fpc", 40), 3)` to
`r f(s1_cell("gamma", "fix_cl2e_b", "binomial", "fpc", 40), 3)`. Under independent errors the binary
$\alpha(t)$ at $G = 40$ stays below nominal with fixed smoothing parameters
(`r f(s1_cell("alpha", "fix_cl2e_b", "binomial", "iid", 40), 3)`).

```{r}
#| label: fig-s1-alpha-gamma
#| fig-cap: "Covariance components, intercept $\\alpha(t)$ and coefficient function $\\gamma(t)$: grid-averaged coverage of nominal 95% pointwise intervals, settings and marks as in @fig-s1-beta; model-based ($\\mathbf V_c$), CR1 and CL2 (Bayesian form), and CL2 after a refit with smoothing parameters fixed at the setting's geometric-mean REML values."
#| fig-height: 6.6
fig_s1_cov(s1_long(s1_cells, s1_arms |> filter(arm %in% c("model", "cr1_b", "cl2e_b", "fix_cl2e_b"), crit == "z"), c("alpha", "gamma")), c("est", "error"))
```

## Satterthwaite degrees of freedom

For a contrast $\mathbf a^\top\boldsymbol\theta$ the sandwich part of @eq-s1-cl2 is a quadratic form
in the whitened residuals, $\mathbf a^\top\mathbf V_p(\sum_i\mathbf U_i\mathbf U_i^\top)\mathbf V_p\mathbf a = \sum_i (\mathbf q_i^\top\mathbf z_i)^2$
with $\mathbf q_i = \mathbf R_i^{-1/2}\tilde{\mathbf X}_i\mathbf V_p\mathbf a$ (times $G/(G-1)$). Under the
Gaussian working model with fixed smoothing parameters, $\mathbf z = (\mathbf I - \tilde{\mathbf H})\boldsymbol\varepsilon$
with independent errors. The quadratic form then has mean $\operatorname{tr}\boldsymbol\Gamma$ and variance
$2\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol\Gamma^2)$, where the $G \times G$ matrix $\boldsymbol\Gamma$ has entries
$\Gamma_{ih} = \mathbf q_i^\top[(\mathbf I - \tilde{\mathbf H})(\mathbf I - \tilde{\mathbf H})^\top]_{ih}\mathbf q_h$.
Matching a scaled $\chi^2_\nu$ gives the Satterthwaite degrees of freedom
$$
\nu(\mathbf a) = \frac{(\operatorname{tr}\boldsymbol\Gamma)^2}{\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol\Gamma^2)}
$$ {#eq-s1-satt}
[@BellMcCaffrey2002; @PustejovskyTipton2018], computed for every evaluation point; the interval
uses $t_{\nu, 0.975}$ in place of $z_{0.975}$. The Satterthwaite intervals evaluated here compute
@eq-s1-satt for the sandwich part only. A variant matches the moments of the full Bayesian CL2 variance,
whose term $\mathbf a^\top(\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_e)\mathbf a$ is fixed, which increases $\nu$.
Using only the diagonal of $\boldsymbol\Gamma$ gives practically the same $\nu$.

The Satterthwaite intervals use the REML fits and CL2 covariances of Appendix A.6 (the `r n_distinct(SAT$cell)`
main factorial settings at the default signal level, `r unique(SAT$n_rep)` replicates); @sec-res-intervals,
@sec-plasmode-results and Supplement S1.2, S1.7 and S2.1 give them with 20 curves, in the extensions and on the
plasmode data.

The median
per-point degrees of freedom are `r rng(SATD$df_median[SATD$G == 40], 0)` with $G = 40$ curves and
`r rng(SATD$df_median[SATD$G == 100], 0)` with $G = 100$; across both, that is
`r rng(SATD$df_median_rel, 2)` times $G - 1$.

Under dependent errors, Satterthwaite intervals cover the
mean, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ at `r rng(satv("satt", 40))` with 40 curves (normal critical value:
`r rng(satv("z", 40))`) and at `r rng(satv("satt", 100))` with 100 (`r rng(satv("z", 100))`), at
`r rng(satv("satt", 40, col = "wr"), 2)` and `r rng(satv("satt", 100, col = "wr"), 2)` times the width
with the normal critical value (@fig-s1-satt).

Satterthwaite intervals do not repair the binary intercept: they cover `r rng(satv("satt", c(40, 100), "alpha", fam = "binomial"))`
under dependence and `r rng(satv("satt", c(40, 100), "alpha", "independent", fam = "binomial"))` under
independent errors. For this term the Satterthwaite degrees of freedom are large (the intervals widen
by a factor of only `r rng(satv("satt", c(40, 100), "alpha", fam = "binomial", col = "wr"), 2)`), so the reference
distribution cannot make up for a standard error that is too small under independent errors or for the
additional shift of the studentized error under dependence (@sec-res-intervals, Supplement S1.4).

Under independent errors Satterthwaite intervals overcover $\beta$ further
(`r rng(satv("satt", c(40, 100), "beta", "independent"))`). The variant whose degrees of freedom include
$\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_e$ lies between $t_{G-1}$ and the plain Satterthwaite reference.

*Non-Gaussian responses.* We use the same $\nu$ for all families (@sec-cl2), although its derivation
assumes Gaussian errors. Let the entries of $\boldsymbol\varepsilon$ be independent standardized score
contributions with excess kurtosis $\kappa_k$ (for Poisson responses, $\kappa_k = 1/\mu_k$), and let
$\mathbf Q$ be the matrix with $G$ columns whose $i$th column holds $\mathbf q_i$ in the rows of curve $i$
and zeros elsewhere. With $\mathbf B = (\mathbf I - \tilde{\mathbf H})^\top\mathbf Q\mathbf Q^\top(\mathbf I - \tilde{\mathbf H})$,
the quadratic form has, to first order, the same mean $\operatorname{tr}\boldsymbol\Gamma$ but variance
$2\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol\Gamma^2) + \sum_k \kappa_k B_{kk}^2$. Positive excess kurtosis therefore
makes @eq-s1-satt too large and the interval too narrow, and negative excess kurtosis does the reverse.
The size of the extra term depends on $\sum_k B_{kk}^2/\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol\Gamma^2) \le 1$. If
$\tilde{\mathbf H}$ is ignored, this ratio is $1/D$ when all entries of the $\mathbf q_i$ have the same
magnitude, so we expect little effect for contrasts that load on many grid points, unless $\kappa_k$
is comparable to $D$. Sparse grids, localized contrasts and rare binary events are the less favorable
cases. We did not compute this term or evaluate a family-dependent $\nu$. Empirically, under dependent
errors with 40 curves, Satterthwaite intervals cover the mean, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ at
`r rng(satv("satt", 40, fam = "gaussian"))` for Gaussian, `r rng(satv("satt", 40, fam = "poisson"))` for
Poisson and `r rng(satv("satt", 40, fam = "binomial"))` for binary responses.

```{r}
#| label: fig-s1-satt

The 5% quantile of pointwise coverage and the width relative to the normal critical value are in Supplement S7."
